sentences.text: The genus Tetronarce, which includes species commonly known as electric rays, was first described by T. N. Gill in 1862.
These animals belong to the class Chondrichthyes, the order Torpediniformes, and the family Torpedinidae.
While the genus contains nine recognized species, some can reach a total length of 180 cm, a size significantly larger than the 25 to 80 cm range typical of the related genus Torpedo.
However, a Spanish source lists thirteen species within the genus, suggesting ongoing taxonomic discussion.
These rays are slow-moving bottom-dwellers that uniquely use electricity for both defense and feeding.
Despite their modern presence, no fossil occurrences for the genus Tetronarce have been recorded in the Paleobiology Database.
Tetronarce californica is found in the northeastern Pacific Ocean, ranging from Baja California to British Columbia.
Tetronarce cowleyi is distributed around southern Africa, from Walvis Bay in Namibia to Algoa Bay in South Africa.
Tetronarce fairchildi is endemic to New Zealand.
Tetronarce formosa is found in the Northwest Pacific, specifically in Taiwan.
Tetronarce macneilli inhabits southern Australia, ranging from Port Hedland to the Swain Reefs.
Tetronarce nobiliana is found in the Atlantic Ocean, ranging from Nova Scotia to Brazil in the west and from Scotland to West Africa and southern Africa in the east.
Tetronarce puelcha is found in Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay.
Tetronarce tokionis is found in Japan and Taiwan.
Tetronarce tremens is distributed across Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, and Peru.
Tetronarce ramanamurthyi is found in the Southeastern Arabian Sea.
